strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel variation on the classical sequential social learning (herding/cascade) model: a central planner that controls the precision of agents' private signals at a cost, formulated as an infinite-horizon discounted MDP over the public belief. This is a clean and well-motivated extension that, to the best of my knowledge, has not been studied in this form.

Two planner objectives (altruistic maximizing social welfare vs. biased inducing a specific action) are treated systematically, and the resulting optimal policies are structurally characterized, including a six-regime threshold characterization of the biased planner's policy. The qualitative interpretations of these regimes (e.g., last-ditch investment to escape an unfavorable cascade, deliberately degrading precision to maintain a favorable cascade) are insightful and go beyond common intuition.

The convexity of the altruistic value function (Theorem 2) is a technically nontrivial result, since Bayesian belief updates and the action-dependence of future rewards break standard tools (e.g., the Monotone Likelihood Ratio property). The inductive proof strategy over a decision tree exploiting the martingale property of belief updates is credible.

The model is deliberately and explicitly restricted (planner has no private information, signals are truthful and symmetric, control is observable), and the paper convincingly argues that even under these constraints planners can substantially steer social learning (up to ~26% welfare decrease for the biased planner). This strengthens the paper's central message about manipulation of social learning.

The applications (targeted digital ads, persuasive LLM responses) are topical and connect the abstract model to current policy-relevant phenomena, including algorithmic platforms and LLM information providers.
The paper is clearly written, with a good balance of intuition and formalism, and honest discussion of model limitations (Section V).
weaknesses: Complete proofs are not included: the paper explicitly states that all proofs, including the technically involved convexity result (Theorem 2), appear only in a companion/technical report [25] and are merely sketched here. For a theory paper whose main contribution is the characterization of optimal policies, the key results are not verifiable from the manuscript itself, which weakens technical soundness assessment and self-containedness.

Theorem 7 (the main biased-policy characterization) is stated only for a specific range of public belief (b in [0, p]), with the rest of the belief space left as bounds/propositions (D)-(F) rather than a full characterization. Several results are stated as existence claims with unspecified threshold values, limiting the sharpness of the contribution.

The numerical evaluation is quite limited: it assumes a linear cost function β(|q−p|) = k|q−p|, fixes C = 1, uses a single baseline precision (p = 0.7) and discount factor (δ = 0.75) for the depicted examples, and only the linear-cost family is swept. There is no sensitivity analysis over cost shapes (e.g., convex/concave costs), which is important because the structural results depend on β's properties.

The quantitative claims (e.g., the ~80% gap between myopic and optimal altruistic policies interpreted as a price of anarchy, −26.34%/+96.97% welfare changes) rest on a single simulation configuration and are not connected to the theoretical bounds; there is no validation that the numerics match the analytically characterized policy structure beyond the one example in Figure 2.

The model's restrictive assumptions are acknowledged but not relaxed even partially. In particular, the requirement that the planner's information set equals the agents' (no private knowledge of the state) and that all control is observable substantially limits realism of the motivating applications (political campaigns and LLM providers typically do have informational advantages and act non-transparently). No result probes robustness to relaxing even one assumption.

Positioning relative to information-design/Bayesian persuasion literature (e.g., Kamenica–Gentzkow style mechanism design over information structures) is thin; the relationship between 'precision control' and more general information design is not discussed, which affects the perceived novelty of the contribution beyond the specific social-learning setting.

Figure 1 aggregates only one instance of trajectories and parameter choices; error bars, distributional information, and behavior across belief initializations are not reported, weakening the empirical support for welfare claims.

strengths: The paper introduces a novel and well-motivated variation on the classical sequential social learning model (Bikhchandani-Hirshleifer-Welch / Banerjee), in which a planner controls the precision of agents' private signals at a cost, framing social learning control as an infinite-horizon discounted MDP.

The two planner objectives (altruistic vs. biased) are cleanly distinguished, and the model yields interpretable structural results: threshold-form myopic policies, convexity of the value function, and a three-phase optimal altruistic policy with an interesting 'invest in precision only when the public belief is sufficiently uncertain' structure.

The convexity proof technique (induction over a decision tree of signal realizations, exploiting the martingale property of Bayesian updates where standard Monotone Likelihood Ratio arguments fail) appears to be a genuine technical contribution.
Positioning against related work ([17], [18]-[20]) is careful, and the paper is honest about its modeling limitations (equivalent information, symmetric signals, observable control).
The writing is generally clear and the paper is well organized.
weaknesses: Complete proofs are outsourced to a companion reference ([25]) due to space constraints; only proof sketches are provided. For the paper's central technical claims (Theorems 2, 4, 5, 7), this makes the contribution essentially unverifiable from the manuscript alone, which is a serious problem for a standalone submission.

The characterization of the optimal biased planner is only partial: Theorem 7 gives bounds or coarse descriptions (e.g., case (C) states the optimal precision lies in an interval, and an epsilon-perturbation appears in case (E)) rather than an exact policy, weakening the headline claim that biased policies are 'fully characterized'.

The numerical evaluation is thin: a single linear cost function, a single value of C, one discount factor for the illustrated policies, and only four aggregate bars (Fig. 1). There is no sensitivity analysis over k, C, delta, or cost curvature, no statistical reporting beyond averages, and no baselines beyond the null policy. The claim that the myopic-vs-optimal welfare gap is a 'price of anarchy' is loose, since it reflects planner discounting rather than strategic decentralization.

The model is highly stylized relative to its motivating applications: binary state and action, symmetric uncompromised signals, publicly known precisions, and a planner with no informational advantage. The targeted-ads and LLM narratives in Section I-B are loose and partly hand-wavy (e.g., the argument that a less precise signal is more likely to induce backing a losing candidate relies on obfuscation reasoning not formalized in the model), so the practical significance of the results is not well established.

The novelty relative to prior work on controlled social learning ([17], [20]) is incremental in kind (changing the planner's lever from payments/actions to information precision), and the paper does not quantify what new phenomena arise that could not be anticipated from that literature.

Several claims rest on unstated assumptions or conventions (e.g., the cost function is assumed strictly increasing and convex in places but the numerics use a linear cost; the relation between the assumed cost class and the derived threshold structure is not explored).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated model: augmenting classical sequential (Bayesian) social learning with a central planner who controls private signal precisions under convex costs is a fresh control formulation, distinct from prior work on persuasion ([20]) and self-interested coordinators ([17]), as clearly positioned in the related work.

Substantive theoretical contributions: a rigorous characterization of optimal policies for both altruistic (Theorems 1, 2, 4) and biased planners (Theorems 5, 7), with the convexity of the value function being a non-trivial technical result requiring an inductive argument over the belief-update tree since standard MDP results (e.g., monotone likelihood ratio) do not apply.

Rich structural insights: the three-phase optimal altruistic policy and six-phase biased policy go beyond common intuitions (e.g., the planner deliberately reducing precision to keep agents in a cascade), which is genuinely illuminating about manipulation dynamics.

Topical and relevant applications (targeted ads, persuasive LLMs) with an honest and careful discussion of the model's limitations (equivalent information, symmetric signals, observable control), which strengthens credibility.

Interesting welfare analysis: Theorem 8 (monotonicity of welfare in precision) and the numerical 'price of anarchy' comparison between myopic and optimal altruistic policies (~80%) provide a tangible takeaway.
weaknesses: Incomplete proofs in the manuscript: the central convexity result (Theorem 2) is only sketched, with complete proofs deferred to [25] due to space constraints. For the paper's foundational theorem, this weakens self-containedness and verifiability at the venue.

Thin numerical evaluation: experiments use only one cost structure (linear), one baseline precision, one cost of incorrect action, and one discount factor; conclusions like '-26.34% / 96.97%' come from a single parameter instance. No sensitivity analysis, no validation of the threshold-structure theorems against simulations, and no real-world data or calibration.

Restrictive modeling assumptions limit applicability: binary state, binary symmetric signals, exogenous agent ordering, planner cannot cherry-pick signal realizations, and agents know the chosen precision. While acknowledged, these substantially narrow the gap to the motivating applications (ads, LLMs), where planners often do have asymmetric information and can shape content selectively.

The theoretical results rely on structural assumptions (strictly increasing, convex cost β) whose necessity is not explored; robustness of the phase structure to, e.g., non-convex or concave costs is not discussed.

Limited discussion of mitigations: the paper identifies the possibility of welfare-damaging biased planners but offers no analysis of mechanism or policy interventions, leaving the practical significance of the manipulation results somewhat open.

strengths: Novel and timely framework: the paper introduces a genuinely new optimization problem — a centralized information mediator controlling signal precision in a sequential social learning setting — bridging information design (Bayesian persuasion) and controlled social learning, both well-motivated by the rise of LLM-based recommendation and mediation systems.

Substantive theoretical contributions: the proof of convexity of the altruistic value function (Theorem 2) is non-trivial and the decision-tree/martingale technique is likely of independent interest. The characterizations of optimal policies for both altruistic and biased planners (Theorems 1, 3, 4, 5) are careful, including the subtle and honest treatment of non-existence of optimal policies and ϵ-optimal policies in the biased case (Theorems 4D, 5E, Remark 4), which reflects technical maturity rather than hand-waving.

Interesting qualitative insights: the biased planner's strategic modes (last-ditch investment near unfavorable cascades, deliberate obfuscation via precision reduction) and the result that welfare manipulation is possible even under strict transparency constraints (no lying, no cherry-picking, full observability) are policy-relevant findings.

A thoughtful LLM-based empirical component: the paper does not merely claim LLMs are strategic; it (a) isolates non-Bayesian belief-updating biases in LLM agents, (b) structurally validates emergent LLM planner behavior against the analytical optimum, and (c) demonstrates the brittleness of Bayes-optimal policies when applied to non-Bayesian agents (hybrid setting) — a genuinely informative experiment.
Clear writing, honest assumptions discussion (Remark 2), and reasonable positioning against related work in social learning, information design, and LLM agents.
weaknesses: Restrictive modeling assumptions limit external validity: binary symmetric signals, precision fully observable by all agents, planner shares the exact public history, concave costs, and homogeneous agent utilities. Realistic LLM mediators can cherry-pick, frame, or be covert; the paper acknowledges this (Remark 2) but the gap between model and motivating applications is substantial.

The LLM experiments are small-scale and weakly controlled: a single model (EXAONE Deep 32B), a single scenario (car buying), short horizons (~10 agents), and no systematic statistical reporting (seeds, confidence intervals, number of runs). The claimed 'emergent strategic behavior' rests on qualitative structural comparison of policy curves (Figure 2a) rather than rigorous quantitative tests.

A key validity concern: the oracle translates a chosen numeric precision qi into a textual message, but the paper provides no measurement verifying that generated messages actually realize the requested precision (i.e., that the induced belief shift matches qi). If the oracle systematically miscalibrates messages, comparisons between LLM policies and the analytical optimum conflate planner strategy with oracle noise.

Discount factor inconsistencies: theory requires δ ∈ [0, 1) for contraction/MDP results, yet Table 1 includes δ = 1 in experiments without discussion of how the analytically optimal policy is computed at δ = 1.

The convexity result and threshold policy structure, while carefully proven, are close in spirit to existing structural results in Bayesian control and persuasion (e.g., Nyarko 1994, Kamenica & Gentzkow); the increment is real but mostly in the coupling with cascades, and the main theorems are qualitative (existence of thresholds dA, tA) without closed-form characterization.

Ethical/societal implications are invoked heavily in framing (manipulation, steering public opinion) but the paper offers no concrete mitigation or regulatory analysis, deferring this entirely to future work.
Some experimental claims (e.g., '40 to 50% welfare decrease') depend on a single fixed true state (ω = B) and specific parameter sweeps; robustness across states and cost functions is not shown.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel combination of controlled information design and sequential social learning, formalized as an infinite-horizon discounted MDP over public belief, which is well-motivated by the growing deployment of LLMs as information mediators.

The theoretical contribution is substantial and rigorous: the proof of convexity of the altruistic value function (Theorem 2, Appendix C.3) handles the non-trivial interaction between agents' actions and the public belief process via a careful decision-tree argument, and the characterizations of optimal altruistic and biased policies (Theorems 3-5), including the existence/non-existence of optimal policies in regimes, are carefully derived.

The LLM experiments are thoughtfully designed in structure, with three roles (planner, agent, oracle), a hybrid setting to isolate the cost of a miscalibrated Bayesian model, and a decomposition of non-Bayesian behaviors (NB1-NB3) that connects micro-level biases to macro-level belief trajectories.

The analysis of the biased planner, including regimes where the planner intentionally degrades signal precision to induce desired actions even under transparency constraints, is an interesting and policy-relevant finding.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is thin and potentially confounded: a single LLM (EXAONE Deep 32B) is used for all three roles, and 'beliefs' are taken from the model's self-reported JSON probability outputs, which are not a validated measure of internal belief. The claim that LLM agents are 'non-Bayesian' rests on this unverified measurement.

The belief oracle is an artificial construct: whether a textual message can actually realize a prescribed precision q (a probability that the message leaves the buyer with the correct impression) is never verified, so the mapping between the theory's signal model and the LLM simulation is loose and unvalidated.

The generality of the results is unclear: only one scenario (car purchasing), a narrow parameter grid, and a single true-state fixed for the welfare experiments. Claims about 'emergent strategic behavior' of LLMs broadly would require multiple models, multiple scenarios, and ablations over prompt framing, which are absent.

The characterization theorems are largely existence-type results (thresholds dA, tA, t1-t5 exist but are not computed in closed form), which limits the practical predictive power of the theory; quantitative comparisons with the LLM planner are therefore mostly qualitative, and figure 2a/2c are dense and hard to interpret.

Several modeling assumptions are strong and under-justified against real deployments: agents observe the planner's chosen precision exactly, all parties share the same history, the state is binary with symmetric binary signals, and the planner cannot falsify or cherry-pick. Remark 2 acknowledges these, but the paper's societal-risk claims (e.g., 40-50% welfare reduction) extrapolate beyond what these assumptions support.

The reported structural similarity between LLM and optimal policies is claimed despite agents demonstrably violating the Bayesian model on which optimality is defined, so it is not clear what 'optimality' benchmark the LLM planner is being compared against in the LLM-agent setting; the deviations are explained post-hoc rather than predicted.

There are presentation issues, including typos in theorems/proofs (e.g., 'pi0B' in Appendix C.7, 'the final term of this product which can be either' repetition, 'mesage' in the oracle prompt), and some notation abuse (VB(b,q) redefined in C.8) that complicates verification of the already long proofs.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel problem formulation: a centralized planner that strategically controls the precision of private signals in a sequential social learning setting. This sits at a productive intersection of information design (Bayesian persuasion), control of social learning, and LLM-based simulation, and the paper positions itself well against the closest prior work (Wei & Anastasopoulos 2022; Dutting et al. 2025).

The theoretical contributions are substantive: the convexity proof of the altruistic value function (Theorem 2) is non-trivial given that agents' actions depend on the public belief, and the full proofs in the appendix are detailed and appear careful. The characterization of optimal policies for both altruistic and biased planners (Theorems 1, 3, 4, 5) yields interesting structural insights, including regimes where the biased planner intentionally obfuscates signals even under stringent transparency constraints.

The LLM experiments are a thoughtful complement to the theory. The three-role design (agent, planner, belief oracle) is sensible, and the paper honestly reports deviations between LLM behavior and the Bayesian optimum (central tendency bias, resistance to cascades) rather than overclaiming perfect agreement. The findings that LLM planners capitalize on social learning and that myopic policies substantially underperform are meaningful.
The paper is well-written and clearly structured, with assumptions and limitations acknowledged explicitly (Remark 2) and an extension to heterogeneous agent preferences included.
The topic — algorithmic information mediators steering social learning and public opinion — is timely and of clear societal relevance for an AI venue.
weaknesses: The empirical validation rests on a single LLM (EXAONE Deep 32B) with no comparison across models, no human baseline, and unclear sample sizes/statistical rigor (no error bars or seeds described for the LLM experiments in the main text). Claims about 'emergent strategic behavior' of LLMs would be considerably stronger with multi-model evidence and uncertainty quantification.

The critical link between the theoretical model and the LLM simulation is the belief oracle, which is asked to generate textual messages with a 'prescribed precision.' This mapping is never validated: there is no empirical check that a 'precision q' message actually induces the intended signal informativeness for LLM agents. Without this, structural similarity between LLM planner policies and the theoretical optimum could partially be an artifact of the prompt design.

Experimental parameter choices are limited: a linear cost function is assumed despite the theory allowing general concave costs, discount factors include δ = 1 even though the theory requires δ < 1 for the infinite-horizon discounted objective, and welfare results (Figure 2c) appear to be computed for one fixed true state, limiting the generality of the 40–50% welfare-damage claims.

The theoretical model relies on strong simplifying assumptions (binary state, binary symmetric signals, homogeneous agents, fully observable precision choices, Bayes-rational agents). While the LLM experiments partially address the rationality assumption, the gap between the model and the motivating applications (recommendation systems, political campaigns) remains large, and the practical significance of the threshold-structure results is hard to assess.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: no explicit statement of code or data release, and key experimental details (number of simulated agents per run, number of repetitions) are not specified in the main text.

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence supports — e.g., 'establish our framework as a tractable basis for studying... that corresponds to real behavior' and 'LLMs exhibit sophisticated strategic reasoning' — given that the validation is limited to one model and one task (car purchase) with an unvalidated precision-to-message channel.
